p1.title: Passage 1
paras: India’s New Education Policy (NEP) represents a paradigmatic departure from the colonial legacy of rote memorization toward a holistic, multidisciplinary framework. By restructuring the pedagogical hierarchy from 10+2 to a 5+3+3+4 system, the policy aims to integrate vocational skills with academic rigor, thereby dissolving the rigid silos between arts, sciences, and commerce. The emphasis on mother-tongue instruction in foundational years acknowledges the cognitive benefits of learning in a native language. However, the grandeur of the vision faces the friction of ground realities. The "implementation gap" poses a severe threat; a multidisciplinary approach requires teachers capable of traversing disciplinary boundaries—a resource currently scarce. Without a massive overhaul of infrastructure and teacher training, the NEP risks remaining a visionary document.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The global agricultural sector faces a massive challenge: it must drastically scale food production to meet a growing population while simultaneously cutting its heavy environmental footprint under the pressures of climate change. The twentieth-century Green Revolution relied on intense inputs—using massive amounts of chemical fertilizers, synthetic pesticides, and groundwater pumping—which damaged soil ecology, depleted aquifers, and accelerated biodiversity loss. Continuing with this resource-heavy paradigm is ecologically impossible. Achieving sustainable food security requires adopting smart agricultural innovations, such as precision farming using IoT sensors, developing climate-resilient crop varieties that resist drought, and scaling agroecological farming systems. However, smallholder farmers, who produce the majority of food in developing countries, are often locked out of these technologies due to high costs and lack of credit. True agricultural resilience requires building equitable technology distribution frameworks, offering localized crop insurance against weather shocks, and protecting seed sovereignty for small farmers.

questions.q: The "5+3+3+4 system" mentioned in the passage refers to:
opts: The teacher–student ratio.
The number of languages a student must learn.
The years needed for a PhD.
The new structure of school education.
questions.why: Detail: it replaces the 10+2 'pedagogical hierarchy'. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Civil Registrar-cum-Sub Registrar), Mar 2026.

questions.q: The primary objective of the NEP, as described, is to:
opts: Make English the only medium.
Shift from rote learning to a multidisciplinary, holistic framework.
Keep the colonial legacy.
Separate arts, sciences and commerce more rigidly.
questions.why: Main idea: the first sentence. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Civil Registrar-cum-Sub Registrar), Mar 2026.

questions.q: What is identified as the major challenge to the NEP?
opts: The scarcity of teachers able to teach across disciplines.
Students' lack of interest in vocational skills.
Refusal to use the mother tongue.
Parents' resistance.
questions.why: Detail: the fifth sentence. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Civil Registrar-cum-Sub Registrar), Mar 2026.

questions.q: The phrase "dissolving the rigid silos" means:
opts: Making science harder.
Reducing vocational training.
Breaking down the strict separation between streams of study.
Pulling down old storage buildings.
questions.why: Vocabulary in context: silos between 'arts, sciences, and commerce'. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Civil Registrar-cum-Sub Registrar), Mar 2026.

questions.q: Why does the policy emphasize mother-tongue instruction?
opts: Because of the cognitive benefits of learning in one's native language.
English is too hard for children.
To promote nationalism only.
To cut printing costs.
questions.why: Detail: the third sentence. Passage: GPSC CBRT (Civil Registrar-cum-Sub Registrar), Mar 2026.

questions.q: A major negative legacy of the twentieth-century Green Revolution, according to the passage, is
opts: the end of synthetic pesticide manufacturing
deep environmental damage, including degraded soil and depleted aquifers
a drop in food production that triggered famines
over-reliance on decentralised technology for small farmers
questions.why: Second sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Which is listed as a modern innovation for sustainable food security?
opts: more groundwater pumping with chemical inputs
precision farming with IoT sensors and climate-resilient crop varieties
growing only high-input cash crops
phasing out agroecological farming
questions.why: Fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Smallholder farmers in developing nations struggle to adopt modern agri-tech because of
opts: a preference for chemical-heavy models
high technology costs and lack of credit
state laws banning IoT sensors
absence of weather shocks
questions.why: Fifth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: According to the text, true agricultural resilience requires
opts: shifting all farming to corporate monocultures
ending crop insurance
fair technology distribution, localised insurance and seed sovereignty
using more chemical fertiliser
questions.why: Last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The author's main argument is that food security must be achieved by
opts: expanding Green Revolution methods
balancing higher production with ecological sustainability and smallholder equity
putting corporate profits first
letting climate change improve soils
questions.why: The opening sets the dual goal; the ending adds equity for small farmers. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.
